title: Service Coverage Gap Viewer: Overlaps and Holes
description: Place centres and radii to expose overlaps and gaps with the Service Coverage Gap Viewer — see where service covers, doubles and fails. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two depots 10 miles apart with 10-mile radii overlap by 39.1% of each circle — the viewer turns that statistic into a map you can argue with.
quick_answer: The Service Coverage Gap Viewer lets you place multiple centres and radii and see where coverage overlaps or leaves gaps. Add your depots, hubs or towers and read the map: doubly served ground, singly served ground, and the holes nobody is serving at all.
steps_intro: One circle always looks fine. Two start telling the truth:

Signal coverage has the same geometry: overlap for handover, gaps for dead zones. The map speaks both languages.
Granted territories that overlap breed disputes; gaps are unclaimed market. Both print clearly here.
Stations' response rings over a county: the gap is where the next station belongs — an argument this map makes better than a spreadsheet.

examples.label: Example · How overlap fades with distance

body.t: Two 10-mile circles: centres 5 mi apart overlap 68.5% of each circle; at 10 mi apart, 39.1%; at 14 mi, 18.8%; at 17 mi, 6.8%; at 20 mi they only touch. Spacing decisions live on this curve.
Three circles in a triangle can each overlap their neighbours and still leave a curvy triangular hole in the middle — the classic gap this viewer exists to expose.

popular_table.note: Overlap is not waste by definition — services want some (handover, choice, resilience). The viewer shows the amount; your operation decides how much is design and how much is accident.

faq: Any ground inside your region of interest covered by no circle. The viewer makes gaps visible; whether a gap matters depends on who lives or travels there.
Centres carry their own radii — a flagship's 15-mile ring and a kiosk's 3-mile ring analyse together fine.
How many centres can I place?
Enough for a real network review; beyond a dozen or so, a GIS earns its licence. This viewer owns the planning conversation's scale.
Shares here are quoted per circle. Union coverage (total ground served at least once) is the companion figure the map shows visually.
Real reach follows roads — the drive-time refinement comes after the geometry review, which catches the structural mistakes roads cannot fix.
Where should a new centre go?
In the largest gap's heart, tested by placing it and re-reading the map — the iterate-here loop is the planning method.
This viewer is geometric. Overlaying population is the Buffer & Overlay Analyzer's counting job next door.
Centres and radii are the layout — note them and the map rebuilds exactly.
